title: Does an Executable Generate–Validate–Repair Loop Reduce Semantic Failures in LLM-Generated NetOps Changes?
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) that tested whether inserting an executable emulator validator into a generate→validate→repair pipeline (guarded) reduces semantic/network-level failures versus an LLM-only suggestion workflow (baseline). Using a deterministic paired design with N=120 intent→configuration tasks (40 tasks per topology class: edge, core, leaf–spine) we produced one shared initial candidate per task via gpt-5-mini (model_calls_used = 120) and evaluated that candidate under both conditions. A deterministic emulator validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) enforced structured workflow policies and could trigger ≤1 repair iteration per guarded episode. Observed outcomes: baseline successes = 120/120; guarded successes = 120/120 (n_11=120, n_10=0, n_01=0, n_00=0). Exact two-sided McNemar p = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00; bootstrap-percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Validator traces record repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes. We address reviewer requests by (1) condensing provenance into a compact artifact paragraph, (2) providing a precise formal definition of the binary scoring rule used for the confirmatory McNemar test with a concrete artifact-grounded example, and (3) adding a concise nearest-work comparison matrix that highlights methodological contrasts with the closest prior studies. We expand methodological clarifications, report exact execution accounting, and discuss construct/external validity and design recommendations for future confirmatory studies.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) can translate operator intent into concrete configuration commands but can produce syntactically plausible yet semantically unsafe sequences (for example, changing MTU without required shutdown, or violating group-availability invariants during uplink switchover). Prior work therefore recommends integrating verification, emulation, digital twins, or veto layers so generated candidates are validated before enactment. Evaluating such guarded pipelines requires executable tests that detect sequencing and stateful failures beyond syntax-level checks. We executed a preregistered paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) that isolates the marginal effect of an executable validator and a bounded repair policy on identical generator outputs. Research question: Does integrating an executable network emulator as a validator in a generate→validate→repair pipeline reduce semantic/network-level failures when enacting LLM-generated configuration changes compared to an LLM-only suggestion workflow? Our contributions: (1) a preregistered, artifact-rich paired experiment (N=120) holding the generator fixed and measuring the incremental effect of an executable validator plus bounded repair; (2) precise, artifact-grounded definition of the binary scoring rule used in the confirmatory McNemar test and an illustrative concrete example drawn from archived scoring artifacts; (3) a compact nearest-work comparison matrix contrasting our shared-generation paired design with representative prior studies; and (4) methodological recommendations for follow-up confirmatory designs when generator outputs produce few invalid candidates.
sections.related_work: Two complementary strands frame this study. First, executable-benchmark and NetOps verification work emphasises that text-level correctness does not guarantee safe enactment: closed-loop emulation exposes sequencing and stateful errors—make-before-break mistakes, group-availability violations, and required-ordered operations—that token-level checks miss. Second, tool-augmented agent architectures and bounded-autonomy guardrails (veto layers, canaries, translation-to-formal-model, generate→validate→repair) are widely proposed as operational safety measures. Published surveys and benchmarks recommend integrating verification or emulation but systematic cross-model closed-loop comparisons under identical harnesses remain limited. Table A (nearest-work comparison) succinctly contrasts the closest prior experiments and tool papers with the present design, using verified primary sources. Key distinctions are: (i) our shared-generation paired design holds the generator fixed across compared conditions, (ii) we use an executable emulator validator able to enforce structured workflow policies from the task manifest, and (iii) the guarded arm had an explicit repair budget ≤1 per episode. This contrasts with many prior benchmark studies that either focus on generator performance (sampling/prompt variance) or present prototype tool integrations without isolating validator marginal effects.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and experimental plan. The study was preregistered (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) before execution. Confirmatory design: paired-binary test with exactly N=120 distinct intent→configuration tasks partitioned deterministically into three topology classes (edge/core/leaf–spine; 40 tasks each). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; primary test: exact two-sided McNemar; bootstrap-percentile 95% CI computed with 10,000 resamples (seed = 1729). The preregistration specified deterministic task generation, a repair budget of ≤1 per guarded episode, contamination controls, deterministic emulator resets, explicit exclusion rules, and a sensitivity plan treating technical exclusions as failures.

Task generation and shared-generation design. Tasks were created deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and include: initial_state, expected_final_state, natural-language intent, required_sequence (canonical ordered operations), and difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, required_command_count, difficulty level). For each task we performed a single shared initial candidate generation using the declared model gpt-5-mini (execution manifest: model_calls_used = 120; stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 120}). The paired shared-candidate design isolates validator/repair marginal effects by removing generator variance across paired episodes; the trade-off is under-exercising repairs if the generator commonly produces valid candidates for the chosen bank.

Validator, scorer and repair semantics. The guarded pipeline invoked deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0), an executable emulator/validator applying structured workflow policies present in each task payload (for example: must_be_down_for_fields, final_group_constraints, make-before-break). The validator executes candidates in an emulated state checker and emits validator_trace fields including validation_before, validation_after, observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_count, and repair_applied. The preregistered repair policy invoked at most one repair iteration when validator.violation_count>0 and archived repair prompts/traces whenever produced. In this run validator.violation_count = 0 for all guarded episodes and repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes.

Formal binary scoring rule used for the confirmatory test. To ensure transparency, we define the confirmatory pass/fail mapping used to build the paired contingency table. Let S denote the scorer object and V the validator_trace for a given episode. An episode is scored PASS (coded 1) if and only if all of the following hold: (a) S.scoring_status == "COMPLETED"; (b) S.score == 1; (c) V.validation_after.valid == true; and (d) V.validation_after.violation_count == 0. Otherwise the episode is scored FAIL (coded 0). Tie/partial conditions (for example, S.score == 0.5) were not present in archived scoring artifacts and would be treated as FAIL per preregistration. Concrete artifact-grounded example: execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json shows scoring fields: score = 1; score_reason_code = "VALID_CONFIGURATION"; scoring_status = "COMPLETED"; validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true; validator_trace.validation_after.violation_count = 0; validator_trace.repair_applied = false; normalized_response equals normalized_reference_answer. Under the formal rule above task-000001-baseline is scored PASS (1). The confirmatory McNemar test was performed on these binary labels for each of the 120 paired tasks.

Instrumentation, contamination controls, and reconciliation. The harness enforced deterministic emulator resets (container image checksums + deterministic seeds) between tasks and recorded provider-call audits and contamination heuristics (duplicate-output detection; cross-condition cache reuse). No contamination flags or technical exclusions occurred. Execution manifest summary (archived): planned_episode_count = 240; completed_episode_count = 240; failed_episode_count = 0; model_calls_used = 120; maximum_model_calls = 240; started_at_utc = 2026-08-29T00:39:14.248966+00:00; completed_at_utc = 2026-08-29T00:48:37.619198+00:00. Deterministic_reconciliation confirms all accounting (n_11=120, n_10=0, n_01=0, n_00=0) and provider-call audits (hosted_model_call_event_count = 120; cache_miss_count = 120; cross-condition cache reuse = false).
sections.results:
Execution summary and outcomes. The run completed without exclusions. Condition-level counts (analysis/condition_summary.csv): baseline successes = 120, baseline failures = 0; guarded successes = 120, guarded failures = 0 (success rates = 1.0 for both). Paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv): n_11 = 120, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0. Exact two-sided McNemar test: p = 1.0. Paired-difference estimate = 0.00. Bootstrap-percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.00, 0.00]. Validator traces report repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes, rendering preregistered secondary endpoints concerned with repair incidence vacuous in this run.

Per-topology counts. The deterministic partition (40 tasks per class) produced the following concordant outcomes: Edge: baseline 40/40 success; guarded 40/40 success. Core: baseline 40/40; guarded 40/40. Leaf–spine: baseline 40/40; guarded 40/40. Representative scoring artifacts (for example, execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json and execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json) confirm normalized_response equals normalized_reference_answer and validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true with violation_count = 0.

Diagnostics and reconciliation. analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty; analysis/missingness_summary.csv reports complete_pairs = 120 and zero technical/instrumentation failures. analysis/analysis_log.jsonl records bootstrap parameters (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729) used to compute the degenerate CI. Deterministic_reconciliation.json confirms provider audit counts and pair accounting, supporting integrity of the confirmatory statistics. Because every guarded episode contained no validator-detected violations, no repair_provider_trace artifacts were generated.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation of the ceiling outcome. The paired shared-generation design isolates validator/repair marginal effects by holding generator outputs fixed across conditions. In this task bank and under the frozen prompting strategy for gpt-5-mini, the shared initial candidates satisfied the deterministic emulator validator in all 120 pairs; consequently the guarded pipeline had no opportunity to exercise repair and could not reduce semantic failures relative to baseline. The exact McNemar p = 1.0 and the degenerate bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00] are direct statistical expressions of that ceiling.

Design trade-offs and recommendations. The shared-generation protocol increases internal validity for isolating validator effects but may under-exercise repair when the generator is well-calibrated for the chosen tasks. Archive-derived difficulty metadata (task_manifest entries: dependency_rule_count, required_command_count, difficulty level) indicate many tasks were satisfiable by the frozen prompt. For future confirmatory runs intended to measure repair utility we recommend preregistered adjustments: (1) allow independent generation per condition (or stratified paired blocking) so the guarded arm can intercept generator errors arising from prompt/sampling variance; (2) prespecify controlled prompt perturbations on a subset of tasks to increase generator error incidence while preserving blocks for internal controls; (3) focus confirmatory power on tasks labeled 'very_hard' or with high dependency_rule_count in the manifest to increase probability of generator-induced violations; (4) in exploratory arms, expand repair budget to measure repair convergence and repair-call costs.

Operational implications and auditability. Even when unused, the deterministic validator produced structured traces that improve auditability: recorded fields (which rules were checked, touched fields, why repair was not applied) can support operator explanations and third-party audits. The archived execution artifacts demonstrate end-to-end instrumented accounting suitable for operator-facing explanations and reproducible post-hoc analysis. However, this experiment also highlights that empirical claims about repair benefits require careful experimental framing: if the generator rarely produces invalid candidates under a given prompt for a task bank, the guard will be idle by design.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: strong—deterministic provisioning, exhaustive provider-call audit logs, zero exclusions, and reproducible validator traces. Construct validity: limited by validator policy encodings derived from synthetic task payloads; the validator enforces task-specified rules but does not emulate all vendor-specific behaviors or partial-observability telemetry. External validity: constrained by the synthetic deterministic task corpus, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy. Conclusion validity: preregistered power assumptions (baseline failure ≈0.40; target absolute reduction 0.15) were not met because baseline empirical failure = 0.00, rendering the confirmatory test uninformative for the originally targeted effect size.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment (N=120) comparing an executable generate→validate→repair pipeline against an LLM-only workflow under a deterministic harness with a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini). All 120 shared initial candidates passed the deterministic emulator validator (n_11 = 120), yielding a paired-difference estimate of 0.00 (exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00], 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) and repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes. The primary scientific contribution is methodological: we demonstrate how a preregistered, artifact-rich shared-generation paired design cleanly isolates validator/repair marginal effects and how deterministic archival artifacts (task manifests, validator traces, provider-call audits, and reconciliation files) enable reproducible failure analysis and transparent auditing even when the primary confirmatory test is degenerate. Archived artifacts permit targeted follow-ups (for example, relaxing shared-generation, selecting high-difficulty tasks, expanding repair budgets, or comparing model families) to measure practical repair utility under realistic generator variance.

limitations: Confirmatory scope: results are narrowly scoped to the preregistered synthetic task set, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy; generalization to production heterogeneity is limited.
Synthetic task provenance: tasks were synthetic/deterministic and may underrepresent noisy, adversarial, or multi-vendor production incidents; external validity to live networks is constrained.

Shared-generation design: using a single shared initial generation per paired task isolates validator/repair efficacy but precludes detection of generation-variance effects; this choice contributed to the ceiling outcome and limits inference about repair utility on independently generated invalid outputs.

Validator fidelity: the deterministic emulator/validator is reproducible but simplifies heterogeneity present in multi-vendor, partially observable production environments; some real-world failure modes may not be exposed.

Statistical ceiling: baseline success reached 100% on the tested task bank, violating the preregistered power assumptions (targeted absolute reduction = 0.15) and rendering the McNemar confirmatory test uninformative for demonstrating the preregistered effect size.
